article_title: GitHub Actions Graduates RHEL 9 and RHEL 10 Runner Images to General Availability

content_preview.title: GitHub Actions Graduates RHEL 9 and RHEL 10 Runner Images to General Availability
content_preview.summary: GitHub Actions moved its Red Hat Enterprise Linux 9 and 10 runner images to general availability five months after their preview, as a separate change retires ARM32 job support in December.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Overview

GitHub has moved Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL) 9 and RHEL 10 runner images for GitHub-hosted larger runners out of preview and into general availability. According to [GitHub's changelog](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-11-19-red-hat-enterprise-linux-runner-images-now-generally-available/), the images, built "in partnership with Red Hat," are "now fully supported for production workflows in GitHub Actions," letting teams run continuous-integration jobs "on the same operating sy...

editor_notes.content_quality: Clean, well-structured News piece (530 words, within the 400-1200 range) organized into Overview / What We Know / Context / What We Don't Know. Every specific and every quoted fragment traces to one of the five cited sources; no orphan URLs in the body that are missing from article.sources.
editor_notes.source_verification: All 5 source snapshots (source-0 through source-4) read in full from the gzipped HTML in sources/2026-11/github-actions-graduates-rhel-9-and-rhel-10-runner-images-to-general-availability/. Decompressed sha256 of each file matches manifest.json exactly (95e5a875...3c1f, 6d81e9bb...30a2e, b9ba0681...bca33, e4ecb9ba...9ebd, 2c9c06da...afc3c). source-0 (github.blog, Nov 19, 2026 GA changelog) confirms verbatim: 'in partnership with Red Hat', 'now fully supported for production workflows in GitHub Actions', 'on the same operating system you deploy to', 'If you've been using RHEL images during the public preview, no action is required. Your existing runners and workflows will continue to work as-is.', 'available for larger runners on GitHub Team and GitHub Enterprise Cloud plans', 'under partner images'. source-1 (github.blog, June 25, 2026 preview changelog) confirms the canonical preview date is June 25, 2026 (dateline reads 'June 25, 2026') and the quote 'Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL) 9 and RHEL 10 images in public preview, introduced in partnership with Red Hat' plus 'Linux x64 larger runners' verbatim. source-2 (github.blog, Nov 12, 2026 ARM32 retirement) confirms verbatim 'by 8th Dec 2026' and 'This follows our end of support for node20 where Node 24 does not support ARM32' and 'Join the discussion within GitHub Community'. source-3 (github.blog, Sept 23, 2026 Node 20 retirement) confirms verbatim 'Node 24 is incompatible with macOS 13.4 and earlier, and it doesn't officially support ARM32' and 'Self-hosted runners using these operating systems or architectures are no longer supported' (dated Sept 23, 2026, matching the article's 'two months earlier' relative to the Nov 12 ARM32 notice). source-4 (docs.github.com custom-images doc) confirms verbatim 'only available for organizations and enterprises using the GitHub Team or GitHub Enterprise Cloud plans', the 'pre-warmed' quote with 'allowing workflows to complete quicker, by downloading packages and binaries once during image creation instead of every time a workflow is run', and 'Linux x64, Linux ARM64, or Windows x64' as the three listed custom-image platforms (confirming ARM32's absence from that list, as the article states). github.blog and docs.github.com are both already on config/source_allowlist.txt; no allowlist action needed. manifest.json shows suspicious_patterns: null on all 5 entries — no prompt-injection content found in any snapshot. Anthropic disclosure: not required - subject matter is GitHub Actions/RHEL runner images and an ARM32 retirement tied by GitHub to Node.js; Anthropic is not the subject, and is not referenced in headline, summary, or lead (contributor_model is Claude Sonnet 5, but that is the Herald's own provenance field, not an in-article Anthropic/Claude credit).
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: Quote-by-quote audit: every double-quoted fragment in body_markdown appears verbatim in its cited snapshot (confirmed above). Date-accuracy check specifically requested by the orchestrator: the writer self-reported catching a WebFetch hallucination that had invented 'June 24, 2026' as the preview date; the submitted body correctly reads 'June 25, 2026' in both the 'What We Know' section and implicitly in the Context section's 'five months after its June 2026 preview' — this matches source-1's dateline of June 25, 2026 exactly. Novelty check on the headline's GA claim: source-0 itself frames the Nov 19 change as graduating RHEL images 'Originally introduced in public preview in June 2026... now fully supported for production workflows' — a genuine preview-to-GA state transition, not an overclaim of day-one novelty; the article's headline and body correctly frame GA as following the June preview rather than presenting it as a brand-new feature. The ARM32 retirement is a separate, independently dated and sourced claim (Nov 12, 2026 changelog, 'by 8th Dec 2026') correctly kept apart from the RHEL GA story in its own Context paragraph, with GitHub's own stated causal link to Node 20/24 quoted rather than invented by the writer. No absence/quantifier overclaims found: 'GitHub first introduced' (line 9) is consistent with source-1 being the earliest dated announcement found in the source set; the 'only available for...' quote (line 13) is verbatim, not a Herald-derived generalization. Derived figures ('about five months', 'two months earlier') are reasonable roundings of June 25 -> Nov 19 (~4mo 25d) and Sept 23 -> Nov 12 (~1mo 20d) respectively.
